topic: the concept of terminal velocity and air resistance

options.text: The maximum constant speed a falling object reaches when air resistance balances gravity
options.feedback: Correct -- once these two forces balance, the object stops accelerating and falls at a constant speed.

options.text: The speed at which an object hits the ground
options.feedback: Impact speed depends on the situation and isn't specifically what terminal velocity refers to -- it's about reaching a maximum constant falling speed.

options.text: The initial speed of a falling object
options.feedback: Terminal velocity refers to the object's final, maximum steady speed, not its starting speed.
The speed of sound is an unrelated physical constant, not connected to terminal velocity.

medium.text: A skydiver falls faster and faster after jumping, but eventually stops accelerating and falls at a constant speed. Why does this happen?

options.text: As speed increases, air resistance increases too, until it becomes equal in strength to gravity, resulting in zero net force and constant velocity
options.feedback: Correct -- this balance of forces (gravity down, air resistance up) is exactly what produces terminal velocity.

options.text: Gravity actually stops acting on the skydiver after a certain point
options.feedback: Gravity continues acting throughout the fall -- it's the increasing air resistance that eventually balances it out, not gravity disappearing.

options.text: The skydiver's mass decreases as they fall, reducing the force of gravity
options.feedback: Mass doesn't change during a fall -- terminal velocity results from air resistance increasing to match the (constant) force of gravity.

options.text: Air resistance has no actual connection to a skydiver's falling speed
options.feedback: Air resistance is precisely the force responsible for eventually balancing gravity and producing a constant falling speed.

hard.text: A skydiver falling face-down reaches a certain terminal velocity. If they then reorient into a head-down 'dive' position (reducing their cross-sectional area facing the airflow), how would their new terminal velocity compare, and why?

options.text: It would be higher, since reducing cross-sectional area lowers air resistance at any given speed, requiring a greater speed before air resistance again balances gravity
options.feedback: Correct -- since air resistance depends heavily on the object's cross-sectional area facing the airflow, reducing that area means the diver must fall faster before reaching the new force balance.

options.text: It would be lower, since a head-down position always increases air resistance
options.feedback: This is backwards -- reducing cross-sectional area (as in a head-down dive) actually DECREASES air resistance at a given speed, leading to a HIGHER terminal velocity, not lower.

options.text: It would remain exactly the same, since body orientation has no effect on terminal velocity
options.feedback: Body orientation significantly affects cross-sectional area and thus air resistance, which directly changes the terminal velocity -- it would not stay the same.

options.text: Terminal velocity is a fixed constant that never changes for any object
options.feedback: Terminal velocity actually varies significantly based on factors like shape, orientation, and mass -- it is not a fixed universal constant.

easy.hard: This is the constant speed reached once two opposing forces acting on a falling object reach equilibrium.
easy.medium: This is the top constant speed a falling object reaches once air resistance balances gravity.
easy.easy: This is the top steady speed something reaches while falling.

medium.hard: As velocity increases, drag force grows correspondingly, until it exactly opposes and cancels out the constant gravitational force.
medium.medium: As the skydiver speeds up, the air pushing back gets stronger, until it's finally as strong as gravity pulling down.
medium.easy: As the skydiver speeds up, the air pushing back gets stronger until it matches gravity pulling down.

hard.hard: Since drag force scales with cross-sectional area, reducing that area shifts the speed at which drag force again matches the (unchanged) gravitational force, upward.
hard.medium: With less body area facing the air, there's less resistance at any given speed, so the diver has to go faster before resistance catches up to gravity again.
hard.easy: With less body area facing the air, there's less resistance, so the diver has to go faster before it balances gravity.
